metadata.title: Computer user profiles in early adolescence and digitally assessed mathematics: A latent class analysis

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses INVALSI’s 2019 Field Trial (FT) mathematics assessment for grade 8 in Italy, administered to students in a representative sample of schools and classes (two randomly selected classes within each randomly selected school). The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or any replicate-weight scheme; therefore, it is unclear whether population-representative weighting was applied in estimation. Analyses were conducted in Mplus with robust standard errors to account for non-independence of observations (students clustered within classes), but this is not the same as applying sampling weights. For replication, analysts should check whether INVALSI provides student/class weights for the FT and, if so, apply them consistently with the PV-combining approach used for the mathematics plausible values.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample comprised grade 8 students in Italy who participated in the INVALSI 2019 Field Trial (FT) at the end of the school year. Mathematics tests were administered online using five computer-based test forms (41 items each) randomly assigned to students, together with a short questionnaire. Missingness handling for the LCA indicators was limited to n=5 cases and treated using full information maximum likelihood (FIML) within the unconditional LCA; for auxiliary models, cases with missing values on exogenous sociodemographic variables (n=2) were excluded via listwise deletion.

main_findings.dataset_used: INVALSI 2019 Field Trial Grade 8 Mathematics (digitally assessed mathematics; PVs via AcerConquest)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Latent Class Regression (auxiliary models M1 and M2) — M1: overall Wald χ²(3)=44.20, p<0.001; pairwise mean differences across LCs reported in Table 3. M2: overall Wald χ²(3)=35.61, p<0.001; pairwise mean differences across LCs reported in Table 3. No predictive ML metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) reported because the analysis is mixture-model based rather than supervised ML.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using INVALSI 2019 Field Trial Grade 8 Mathematics the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS), gender, immigrant background, and school geographic location (plus latent computer-user class membership) to analyze mathematics ability (PVs), finding that educational users (LC3) had the highest mathematics PV means and recreational users (LC4) the lowest, with significant omnibus and most pairwise differences even after controlling for sociodemographic variables in model M2. This indicates that supporting adolescents’ learning-oriented computer use patterns may help mitigate achievement disadvantages associated with socioeconomic background, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes heterogeneity in out-of-school computer use among Italian grade 8 students using a person-centered latent class analysis (LCA) and then links latent class membership to digitally assessed mathematics. Mathematics was measured with five online test forms (41 items each) and scaled using a Rasch-calibrated item bank; AcerConquest generated five plausible values (PVs) per student, combined using Rubin’s method in Mplus. The analytic sample included 1,155 students from Italy participating in the INVALSI 2019 Field Trial, with missing LCA indicators handled via full information maximum likelihood and missing exogenous covariates handled via listwise deletion. Four computer-user profiles were retained (sporadic, multipurpose, educational, recreational). Mathematics results showed significant differences across profiles (M1 overall Wald χ²(3)=44.20, p<0.001; M2 overall Wald χ²(3)=35.61, p<0.001), with educational users outperforming other groups and recreational users performing worst; ESCS and gender also had significant direct associations with mathematics. Limitations include the absence of survey-weight reporting and the cross-sectional nature, so associations should not be interpreted as causal effects.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This paper is not an empirical predictive ML study: it uses latent class analysis and auxiliary mixture-model regressions (including multinomial logistic latent class regression) rather than training supervised machine-learning predictors. Consequently, no ML algorithm list, primary ML model, or predictive performance metrics (accuracy/AUC/RMSE) are applicable, and the extraction leaves ml_techniques empty. The main outcomes are mixture-model-based class membership and PV-based mean differences, which are psychometric/mixture modeling rather than ML prediction.
